subject: Mathematics
topic: Derivatives from limits, tangent lines and local estimates
scope: Original AP Calculus AB Unit 2 support for selected points in topics 2.1-2.4. Source: the currently served CED and Fall 2026 corrections, inspected 2026-10-19. Partial topic coverage; no claim of official questions, AP scoring or complete exam preparation.
prerequisites: Evaluate functions and expand polynomial expressions.
Understand a two-sided limit and a secant-line slope.
objectives: Distinguish an average rate from a derivative.
Compute a polynomial derivative from its limit definition.
Construct a tangent line and interpret units.
Explain why a continuous function may lack a derivative.

notes.heading: From an interval to a point
paragraphs: For distinct inputs a and b, the average rate of change is [f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a). It is the slope of the secant through two points on the graph. The numerator measures a change in output and the denominator a change in input, so their units divide. If f is a distance in metres and the input is seconds, the rate is measured in metres per second. An average rate need not equal the rate at either endpoint.

To investigate a rate at a, write b=a+h and consider [f(a+h)-f(a)]/h for nonzero h. The derivative f′(a) is the limit of this quotient as h approaches zero, if a finite two-sided limit exists. We do not set h=0 in the original quotient. The expression is undefined there, but the surrounding values may approach a well-defined limit. Confusing an undefined quotient at zero with a nonexistent limit misses the purpose of the limiting process.

notes.heading: Algebra before the limit
paragraphs: When f(x)=x², expand f(a+h)=(a+h)²=a²+2ah+h². Subtract f(a)=a², factor h from the remaining numerator, and cancel h only while h≠0. The quotient becomes 2a+h, whose limit is 2a. The cancellation does not claim that zero can be divided by zero. It replaces an expression by another with the same values near, but not at, the point used in the limit.

Distinguish f′(a), a derivative value at a fixed input, from f′(x), a new function defined at inputs where the derivative exists. Notations y′ and dy/dx also refer to derivatives when y=f(x). The symbol dy/dx is not an instruction to divide a pair of arbitrary finite changes. At this stage it represents the limit-based local rate. Differentiate the expression with its variable roles intact; constants stay fixed during the limiting process.

notes.heading: Tangents, local prediction and units
paragraphs: If f′(a) exists, the tangent line through (a,f(a)) has equation y-f(a)=f′(a)(x-a). The derivative supplies the slope, but the function supplies the point. Using f′(a) as the vertical coordinate is a common mistake. A tangent can cross a curve elsewhere or even pass through it at the tangency point; tangency is a local slope relationship, not a rule that the line touches the graph only once.

For small changes Δx, the tangent suggests Δy≈f′(a)Δx and f(a+Δx)≈f(a)+f′(a)Δx. This is a local approximation, not generally an equality or a trustworthy long-range forecast. The units provide a check: output per input multiplied by input gives output. A derivative of -3 litres per minute means the volume is decreasing locally at that rate, not that the volume itself is negative.

notes.heading: Estimating from a table
paragraphs: A nearby secant can estimate a derivative when only values are available. A centred difference [f(a+h)-f(a-h)]/(2h) uses points on both sides; a one-sided difference uses a and one neighbour. For a smooth function, shrinking h can improve a suitable estimate, but measured data include rounding and noise. Dividing a small noisy difference by an extremely small h may amplify error. More decimal places do not automatically mean more accurate information.

State whether the result is an estimate and identify the interval used. Irregularly spaced data require the actual change in input, not an assumed constant spacing. A finite table cannot prove that a derivative exists at the target point: many curves, including nonsmooth ones, can pass through the same recorded values. Analytical information or additional assumptions are needed for a rigorous existence claim.

notes.heading: Continuity is necessary, not sufficient
paragraphs: A function differentiable at an interior point is continuous there. One way to see the connection is f(a+h)-f(a)=h times the difference quotient: if the quotient approaches a finite limit, multiplying by h forces the change in f to approach zero. The converse fails. The function |x-2| is continuous at x=2, but its left-hand slope is -1 and its right-hand slope is +1. Since those limits disagree, there is no two-sided derivative at that point.

Corners are not the only obstruction. A discontinuity prevents differentiability, and a vertical tangent does not give a finite derivative under the definition used here. At an endpoint, one-sided derivatives may be discussed if the problem explicitly adopts that convention. Do not silently use a one-sided limit as if it were a two-sided derivative at an interior point. A horizontal tangent, by contrast, can have a perfectly valid derivative equal to zero.

notes.heading: Scope and a reliable solution sequence
paragraphs: This lesson supports selected AP points about difference quotients, derivative notation, tangent lines, estimates and the continuity relationship. The source register identifies the CED pages and the checked 2026 clarification notice. It does not certify every representation or skill in Unit 2 and does not cover the full derivative-rule catalogue. The teaching exercises and one-point-per-criterion rubrics are original, not College Board scoring guidelines.

For a definition problem, write the quotient first, simplify with the nonzero-increment condition, take the limit and interpret the result. For a tangent problem, record both f(a) and f′(a) before writing the line. For a nonexistence claim, name the failed condition and support it with limits or a precise graph feature. Separate exact algebra from numerical evidence so a plausible estimate is not presented as a proof.

notes.heading: Secant error and the choice of a nearby point
paragraphs: A forward difference quotient compares a point with a second point displaced by h. Its value depends on h until a limit is taken. Algebra can reveal exactly how that finite-step estimate differs from the derivative. A centred quotient uses points on both sides; cancellation can remove some error terms, but exactness for one polynomial does not make the method exact for every function. Keep the estimated derivative separate from the function value predicted by a tangent. Both estimates also become sensitive to measurement or rounding error when differences are formed from noisy values. Smaller h reduces a truncation error in an ideal formula, while a practical numerical calculation can have additional errors.

workedExamples.prompt: Find f′(a) from the definition for f(x)=3x²-2x+4.
steps: For h≠0 divide by h to obtain 6a+3h-2.

workedExamples.prompt: Find the tangent line to f(x)=x²+1 at x=3.
steps: The derivative from the square-function calculation is 2x, so the slope is 6.

workedExamples.prompt: A table gives f(1.9)=7.22 and f(2.1)=8.82. Estimate f′(2).
steps: Use the secant between the two nearby inputs.
Label the result as an estimate.
workedExamples.answer: f′(2)≈8; the table alone does not prove differentiability.

workedExamples.prompt: Decide whether f(x)=|x-2| is differentiable at x=2.
steps: f(2)=0 and the difference quotient is |h|/h.
For h<0 the quotient is -1; for h>0 it is +1.
workedExamples.answer: Continuous but not differentiable at x=2.

workedExamples.prompt: For f(x) = x³ at x = 2, simplify [f(2+h)-f(2)]/h for h ≠ 0. Give the derivative and the finite-step estimate at h = 0.1.
workedExamples.answer: The quotient is 12 + 6h + h²; f′(2) = 12; at h = 0.1 the estimate is 12.61.
steps: Subtract 8 and divide by nonzero h to obtain 12 + 6h + h².
The limit is 12; direct substitution of h = 0.1 into the quotient gives 12.61.

misconceptions.claim: The derivative is found by immediately substituting h=0.
misconceptions.correction: Simplify or analyse the nonzero-h quotient, then take its limit.

misconceptions.claim: A continuous graph always has a derivative.
misconceptions.correction: A corner can be continuous while its one-sided slopes disagree.

misconceptions.claim: A tangent must meet the curve only once.
misconceptions.correction: Its defining property is local slope agreement at the point, not a global intersection count.

flashcards.back: Average change per input unit over the interval, for a≠b.

flashcards.front: What is f′(a) in increment notation?
flashcards.back: The limit of [f(a+h)-f(a)]/h as h→0, if it exists as a finite limit.

flashcards.front: Why may h be cancelled in a difference quotient?
flashcards.back: For the nearby values used in the limit, h is nonzero.

flashcards.front: How does f′(x) differ from f′(a)?
flashcards.back: The former is a derivative function; the latter is its value at a fixed point.

flashcards.front: Which point and slope define the tangent at x=a?
If f has units kilograms and x hours, what are derivative units?
Can a finite table prove differentiability?
flashcards.back: No; it supplies estimates unless additional information justifies existence.

flashcards.front: Why does |x| lack a derivative at zero?
flashcards.back: Its one-sided difference-quotient limits are -1 and +1.

flashcards.front: Does differentiability at an interior point imply continuity?
flashcards.back: Yes; the converse need not hold.

flashcards.front: What is the local linear estimate for f(a+Δx)?
flashcards.back: f(a)+f′(a)Δx, with approximation error generally present.

flashcards.front: What is the finite-step error of a derivative estimate?
flashcards.back: The difference between the finite difference quotient and the derivative at the point.

flashcards.front: Does a centred difference always give an exact derivative?
flashcards.back: No. Symmetry can cancel some error terms while leaving others.

questions.prompt: Which expression defines f′(a), provided the limit exists?
questions.answer: lim as h→0 of [f(a+h)-f(a)]/h
solution: A derivative compares nearby output change with input change.
The increment must then approach zero.
markingPoints: Select the limit of the difference quotient.

questions.prompt: For f(x)=2x²+3, calculate f′(4) using a difference quotient.
solution: The quotient simplifies to 4a+2h for h≠0.
Its limit is 4a, which equals 16 at a=4.

questions.prompt: Find the tangent to y=x²-3x at x=2.
solution: Use y+2=x-2.
markingPoints: Obtain the correct point and slope.

questions.prompt: A table gives g(4.8)=10.2 and g(5.2)=11.4. Estimate g′(5) using these values.
solution: The output change is 1.2 and the input change is 0.4.
Divide 1.2 by 0.4 and label the result an estimate.

questions.prompt: Explain why f(x)=|x+1| is continuous but not differentiable at x=-1.
questions.answer: Both sides approach f(-1)=0, but the difference quotient |h|/h tends to -1 from the left and +1 from the right.
solution: Check the function value and limits.
Compute the one-sided quotient limits.
Use their disagreement to reject a two-sided derivative.

questions.prompt: A tank volume satisfies V(2)=40 litres and V′(2)=-3 litres/minute. Give a local estimate for V(2.1).
questions.answer: 39.7 litres.
solution: Use Δt=0.1 minute.
markingPoints: Use the correct small time change.

questions.prompt: A learner finds a centred secant estimate of zero and concludes a graph must be differentiable with a horizontal tangent. Give a counterexample.
questions.answer: For f(x)=|x| about zero, symmetric values are equal, so the centred quotient is zero. The left and right derivatives are -1 and +1, so no derivative exists.
solution: Choose the absolute-value function.
Compute equal symmetric endpoint values.
Compare the one-sided slopes.
markingPoints: Show the centred estimate is zero.

questions.prompt: For f(x)=x², explain why f′(3)=6 does not mean f(3)=6.
questions.answer: f(3)=9 is the function value; f′(3)=6 is the local rate or tangent slope.
solution: Evaluate the original function.
Distinguish the meaning of its derivative value.

questions.prompt: A runner has position s(t)=t²+2t metres. Find the average velocity from t=1 to t=4 seconds.
questions.answer: 7 m/s
solution: s(4)=24 and s(1)=3, so the displacement is 21 metres.
Divide by the elapsed 3 seconds to obtain 7 m/s.
markingPoints: Divide by 3 s and give 7 m/s.

questions.prompt: Interpret lim as h→0 of [(5+h)³-125]/h as a derivative. Identify the function and the input.
questions.answer: f′(5), where f(x)=x³.
solution: The numerator has the form f(5+h)-f(5).
The denominator is the change h, so the limit is the derivative at 5.
markingPoints: Identify the input 5 and the limit as f′(5).

questions.prompt: Use the limit definition to find the derivative of f(x)=1/x at x=2. State the restriction needed when simplifying.
solution: Cancel the nonzero h to obtain -1/[2(2+h)].
Taking h→0 gives -1/4; f itself is undefined at x=0.
markingPoints: Combine fractions and cancel h only for h≠0, with h≠-2.

questions.prompt: Use rationalisation to find the derivative of f(x)=√x at x=9 from first principles.
solution: The quotient is (√(9+h)-3)/h.
Multiply numerator and denominator by √(9+h)+3 to obtain 1/(√(9+h)+3) for nonzero h near zero.
The limit is 1/6.
markingPoints: Rationalise and cancel h with its nonzero restriction.

questions.prompt: A learner says: “The difference quotient is 0/0 at h=0, so x² has no derivative.” Identify and repair the argument.
questions.answer: A limit uses nearby nonzero h; the undefined quotient at zero does not prevent the limit from existing.
solution: Expand ((a+h)²-a²)/h to 2a+h for h≠0.
The simplified expression tends to 2a. No division by zero was performed.
markingPoints: Explain why substitution at h=0 is not the definition of the limit.
Simplify for h≠0 and obtain the limit 2a.

questions.prompt: For f(x)=x², compare the forward and centred difference quotients at x=a. Explain why an exact centred estimate does not prove the same method is exact for every function.
questions.answer: Forward: 2a+h. Centred: 2a. Exactness here follows from cancellation specific to this quadratic.
solution: Expand ((a+h)²-a²)/h to 2a+h.
Expand ((a+h)²-(a-h)²)/(2h) to 2a for h≠0.
For f(x)=x³ the centred quotient is 3a²+h², so a nonzero h leaves an error.
markingPoints: Use the cubic counterexample to limit the claim.

questions.prompt: A graph has a tangent at (3,7) that also passes through (5,1). Find f′(3) and explain why f′(5) cannot be read from this information.
questions.answer: f′(3)=-3; f′(5) is undetermined.
solution: The tangent slope is (1-7)/(5-3)=-3.
The second point is on this tangent, not necessarily on the curve or on its tangent at x=5.
markingPoints: Explain why that slope supplies no derivative value at 5.

questions.prompt: Temperature readings are T(2.7)=21.4°C and T(3.4)=20.0°C, with time in minutes. Estimate T′(3) using this secant and state a limitation.
questions.answer: -2°C/min; an estimate over [2.7,3.4], not an exact instantaneous rate.
solution: The temperature change is -1.4°C and the time change is 0.7 minutes.
Their quotient is -2°C/min. The interval is not centred at 3 and the table alone does not establish the instantaneous slope.
markingPoints: State why this is an estimate.

questions.prompt: A differentiable function has f(2)=5 and f′(2)=0. Must f have a local maximum at x=2? Justify with a function.
questions.answer: No. f(x)=(x-2)³+5 has a horizontal tangent at 2 but no local maximum there.
solution: This function has f(2)=5 and derivative 3(x-2)², giving f′(2)=0.
Values immediately to the left are below 5 and immediately to the right are above 5.
markingPoints: Give a function satisfying both data.
Explain using nearby values why no local maximum is forced.

questions.prompt: Let f(x)=x² for x≤1 and f(x)=ax+b for x>1. Find a and b so that f is differentiable at 1, showing both conditions.
solution: Continuity requires a+b=1 because the left value is 1.
The left derivative at 1 is 2, while the right derivative is a.
Set a=2, then b=1-2=-1.
markingPoints: Obtain b=-1 and satisfy both conditions.

questions.prompt: Let f(x)=x² for x≠1 and f(1)=0. A learner differentiates x² and reports f′(1)=2. Explain why this is invalid.
questions.answer: The changed value makes f discontinuous at 1, so it is not differentiable there.
solution: The limit of f(x) as x→1 is 1 but f(1)=0.
Differentiability implies continuity; a rule valid away from the changed point cannot supply its derivative.
markingPoints: Compare the limit 1 with the actual value 0.
Use failure of continuity to reject a derivative at 1.

questions.prompt: Investigate the derivative of f(x)=x^(1/3) at x=0 using the difference quotient. Distinguish a vertical tangent from a finite derivative.
questions.answer: The quotient h^(-2/3) grows without bound; there is no finite derivative at 0, although the graph has a vertical tangent.
solution: At zero the quotient is h^(1/3)/h=1/h^(2/3) for h≠0.
It tends to positive infinity from either side.
A finite derivative does not exist; continuity at zero is compatible with this vertical tangent.
markingPoints: Form and simplify the difference quotient.
Distinguish the vertical tangent from a finite derivative.

questions.prompt: If C(t) is a concentration in mg/L and t is measured in hours, interpret C′(4)=-0.6 with units.
questions.answer: At 4 hours, concentration is decreasing at an instantaneous rate of 0.6 mg/L per hour.
solution: Derivative units are output units divided by input units: mg/(L·h).
The negative sign indicates a decrease near t=4, not a negative concentration.
markingPoints: Explain the local decrease without asserting a negative concentration.

questions.prompt: A tangent line to y=x² at x=3 is used to estimate f(3.1). Find the absolute difference between the actual function value and this estimate.
solution: The tangent has value 9+6(0.1)=9.6 at 3.1.
The actual value is 3.1²=9.61, giving absolute difference 0.01.

questions.prompt: Why can two smooth curves pass through the same three table points and have different derivatives at the middle point? Give an algebraic construction for points at x=0,1,2.
questions.answer: Add k*x*(x-1)*(x-2) to an interpolating polynomial; it preserves the values but changes the derivative at 1 by -k.
solution: The added term vanishes at 0, 1 and 2, so all three data values stay fixed.
Its derivative at 1 is -k. Choosing different k therefore changes the middle slope.
markingPoints: Construct a term vanishing at all three inputs.
Show its derivative at the middle input need not vanish.

questions.prompt: Prove that differentiability at a implies continuity at a using the difference quotient. Identify the limit assumptions used.
questions.answer: For nonzero h, f(a+h)-f(a)=h*[f(a+h)-f(a)]/h. The second factor has finite limit f′(a), so the product tends to zero.
solution: Differentiability gives a finite two-sided limit of the difference quotient.
For h≠0, multiply that quotient by h to recover f(a+h)-f(a).
By the product limit law, the change tends to 0*f′(a)=0; therefore f(a+h) tends to f(a).
markingPoints: Use the identity for nonzero h.
Apply the product limit law to establish continuity.

questions.prompt: A sensor rounds each reading to the nearest 0.01 unit. Explain why reducing h from 0.1 to 0.0001 in a forward difference need not improve a derivative estimate.
questions.answer: Rounding errors in the numerator are divided by h; a smaller interval can amplify their effect.
solution: Each rounded value may differ by up to 0.005, so the difference can have rounding error up to 0.01.
Dividing this bound by h gives rate-error bounds of 0.1 and 100 respectively. Truncation error may shrink while rounding error grows.
markingPoints: Explain error amplification by division by h.
Compare the bounds 0.1 and 100 without claiming the actual errors reach them.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x³ at x = 2, simplify [f(2+h)-f(2)]/h for h ≠ 0. Give the derivative and the finite-step estimate at h = 0.1.
questions.answer: The quotient is 12 + 6h + h²; f′(2) = 12; at h = 0.1 the estimate is 12.61.
solution: Expand (2+h)³ as 8 + 12h + 6h² + h³.
Subtract 8 and divide by nonzero h to obtain 12 + 6h + h².
The limit is 12; direct substitution of h = 0.1 into the quotient gives 12.61.
markingPoints: Subtract 8 and divide by nonzero h to obtain 12 + 6h + h².
The limit is 12; direct substitution of h = 0.1 into the quotient gives 12.61.

questions.prompt: For the same cubic, a learner says the centred quotient [f(2+h)-f(2-h)]/(2h) must be exactly 12 for every nonzero h. Test that claim algebraically.
questions.answer: The centred quotient is 12 + h², so it approaches 12 but is not exactly 12 for nonzero real h.
solution: Subtract the two cubic expansions to obtain 24h + 2h³.
Divide by 2h to obtain 12 + h².
The linear error cancels, but the h² error remains for nonzero real h.
markingPoints: Subtract the two cubic expansions to obtain 24h + 2h³.
The linear error cancels, but the h² error remains for nonzero real h.

revisionChecklist: Write and simplify the quotient before taking the limit.
Keep point coordinates separate from tangent slope.
Label numerical approximations and their intervals.
Test left/right behaviour before asserting differentiability.
Explain the reasoning in “From secant to derivative for a cubic” and correct the linked error-analysis response without copying its solution.
